facts.claim: UNESCO inscribed 'Dabkeh, traditional dance in Palestine' (State of Palestine) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023 (18.COM).
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/dabkeh-traditional-dance-in-palestine-01998 (read 2026-11-01)

facts.claim: UNESCO: dabkeh is a popular group dance in Palestine accompanied by traditional wind instruments and popular singing, performed during festivals, celebrations and events such as weddings and graduations.
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/dabkeh-traditional-dance-in-palestine-01998 (read 2026-11-01)

facts.claim: UNESCO: dancers stand in a straight line or semicircle, clasping hands and shoulders to show cohesion; the movements involve jumping and hitting the ground with the feet. The UNESCO text describes it as performed regardless of gender (the nomination text says eleven dancers, which refers to the performed group form).
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/dabkeh-traditional-dance-in-palestine-01998 (read 2026-11-01)
facts.conflicts: Britannica (https://www.britannica.com/art/dabkah, read 2026-11-01) says the dabkah is danced mainly by men in the wider region; UNESCO says Palestinian dabkeh is performed regardless of gender. Writer should follow UNESCO for Palestine and not state it is men only.

facts.claim: UNESCO: dabkeh can be performed by professional groups or spontaneously in public squares and family yards; the accompanying folk song lyrics are in local dialects and express emotions tied to the occasion such as courage, strength and love; it is a means of celebrating family occasions and increasing social ties.
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/dabkeh-traditional-dance-in-palestine-01998 (read 2026-11-01)

facts.claim: UNESCO lists nine State of Palestine elements on the Representative List, including The art of embroidery in Palestine (2021), Dabkeh, traditional dance in Palestine (2023) and the multinational Henna: rituals, aesthetic and social practices (2024).
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/state/palestine-PS?info=elements-on-the-lists (read 2026-11-01)

facts.claim: Britannica: dabkah is common in festivities in the area between northern Syria and southern Israel; in Lebanon it is called the national dance, alongside zajal (folk poetry).
facts.source: https://www.britannica.com/art/dabkah (read 2026-11-01)

facts.claim: Palestinian weddings have their own distinctive music, especially the dabke; wedding singers draw on a repertoire including henna songs sung at the henna ceremony, wedding processionals (zeffat) and dabke and dance songs.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)

facts.claim: Traditional Palestinian songs have a set rhythm rather than set lyrics; singers, usually family members or close friends, make up the words on the spot, so lyrics differ from city to city.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)

facts.claim: Ataaba (also atab or mejana) is described as the most popular song type in Palestine; weddings are its main setting. The singer opens with a long 'ooff' sound and the verse has four lines, the first three ending on the same-sounding word with different meanings.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)

facts.claim: Dal'ouna (dal'ona) is the second most popular song form, four lines of verse; it is the sound of the dabke, sung by the dancers to the shubbabah (flute), yarghoul or mijwiz.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)
facts.conflicts: Instruments named by Wikipedia (shubbabah, yarghoul, mijwiz) are wind instruments; UNESCO (fact_104) only says 'traditional wind instruments'. Tabl and mizmar for the zaffeh are NOT confirmed by any source read in this batch.

facts.claim: Sahja is a popular wedding song form with clapping to the rhythm, sung to the bride by women or to the groom by men; the men gather in two lines facing each other or around the groom, and a lead singer (the zajal, a talented singer or close family member) improvises a verse that the group repeats.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia uses 'zajal' for the lead singer; Britannica (fact_108) and common usage treat zajal as a form of folk poetry. Writer: describe zajal as improvised sung folk poetry and the lead as a poet-singer, not as a fixed rank. Timing 'the night before' is NOT sourced.

facts.claim: Zaghareet are among the oldest Palestinian song forms, traditionally sung by women at weddings and important events: one woman opens with a call, adds a short poem or a few rhyming words, then the women join in a long trilling ululation; women take turns and there is no clapping.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Palestine (read 2026-11-01; encyclopaedia, lower confidence: section cites 'Palestinian Popular Songs' with no named author)

facts.source: https://palarchive.org (Palestinian Museum Digital Archive; seen as a Google result via DataForSEO 2026-11-01, page not fetched)

insider_details.detail: Dabkeh is danced in a straight line or semicircle with linked hands and shoulders, jumping and stamping, so ask for a solid dance floor long enough for a line of dancers rather than a small square in front of the band.

Because dabkeh is often danced spontaneously by guests of every age, not only by a hired troupe, plan the floor and sound for everyone joining in, and confirm the venue's sound limit before booking live drums and wind instruments.

Palestinian wedding songs have set rhythms but improvised words from family and friends, so build time into the run sheet for guest-led singing (sahja, zaghareet) rather than treating music as a fixed playlist.
The zaffe is a wedding march, so it needs a route: agree with the venue where the procession forms, the path it takes and where the couple arrives before the music starts.

For couples planning abroad, the UAE sits at Exercise a high degree of caution on Smartraveller, while Palestine is Do not travel and Jordan is Reconsider your need to travel, as at November 2026; the Wedded Advisor confirms current advice before any booking.
